s: Principles worth internalizing.
Structure protects liberty.
Federalism and separation of powers are not just allocations of authority.
They are designed to protect individuals by diffusing power (Bond v. United States, 2011: individuals may raise federalism claims; Free Enterprise Fund).
Rights generally require state action, but Congress can reach private conduct through other powers, notably the Commerce Clause and the Thirteenth Amendment.
The level of scrutiny usually decides the case, so the fight is often over classification and framing.
Is the law sex-based or age-based?
Is the right "marriage," or a more specific claim?
Facial versus as-applied.
A facial challenge must show the law is unconstitutional in all or a substantial number of its applications.
That is the Salerno standard; overbreadth applies in speech cases (Moody v. NetChoice, 2024).
As-applied challenges are narrower and favored.
Remedies are distinct from rights.
Severability: courts excise the invalid provision if the rest can function (Seila Law; Barr v. AAPC, 2020).
Universal injunctions are generally unavailable (Trump v. CASA, 2025).
Ex parte Young, § 1983, and Bivens (now nearly closed to new contexts, Egbert v. Boule, 2022) define who can be sued for what.
Doctrine is historically contingent.
Lemon, Chevron, Roe and Quill all fell within a decade.
Track controlling precedent and its subsequent treatment rather than memorizing tests as timeless.
Distinguish the layers.
Separate the constitutional rule, the statutory overlay (RFRA, the Voting Rights Act, Title VII, § 1983), and prudential or policy arguments.
Constitutional avoidance.
Courts construe statutes to avoid serious constitutional questions where fairly possible (NFIB; Bond), which often means the real constitutional question goes undecided.
